多塔爾琴名稱源自波斯語「二弦」，15世紀起源於伊朗與中亞，最初為牧羊人樂器，琴弦: The name dotar comes from the Persian for “two strings”. It originated in Iran and Central Asia in the fifteenth century as a shepherd's instrument with strings of animal gut. After the Silk Road opened, Chinese silk thread was used instead, and modern instruments usually have nylon or steel strings. It spread to Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and the Uyghur regions of western China; the Herat version has fourteen strings, and in West Bengal and Bangladesh the instrument is called the dotara, some of them with four strings. In the 1920s the musicologist Viktor Belyayev documented the Turkmen form; in modern practice it has moved from accompanying a solo singer to ensembles and purely instrumental music, and Khorasan bakhshi music is on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
多塔爾琴屬弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號321.322。來源記載: The dotar is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322. The source records that the body is burnt and hollowed out of a single block of mulberry and is pear-shaped; the neck is ideally apricot, and modern instruments also use apricot, mulberry or walnut. The strings, the sounding body, were animal gut at first and later silk; the Turkmen tradition uses raw silk and modern instruments mostly nylon or steel. Of the other parts, the thirteen frets are low metal frets and modern instruments have steel tuning pegs; the materials of the remaining parts are not stated.
多塔爾琴屬弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號321.322，為伊朗與: The dotar is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322, a long-necked two-string lute of Iran and Central Asia. Its timbre is warm and soft, and the usual tuning is la–re; the Turkmen form is lower and the two strings are often tuned a fourth apart. It is not sounded with a pick but by striking the strings quickly with the fingers; because the sound is soft, the player has to keep up a dense, repeated striking to sustain it. Compared with related instruments, it is not plucked like the guitar or the mandolin, and it is kin to the Kazakh dombra; the Herat type in Afghanistan can have fourteen strings, and some dotaras in South Asia have four.

It is popular in Tajikistan and in Iran's Khorasan province and is an important instrument of the Turkic peoples of Khorasan; local players are called bakhshi, and their Khorasan bakhshi music is on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The Turkmen dotar was at first a solo instrument accompanying a singer and later entered ensembles and purely instrumental pieces. Uyghurs in western China mostly pluck it, while Tajiks, Turkmens and Uzbeks use both strumming and plucking.

The dotar is a long-necked two-string lute found in Iran and Central Asia, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322. The body is mostly pear-shaped and the instrument is about one to two metres long; Uyghurs mostly pluck it, while Tajiks, Uzbeks and Turkmens use both strumming and plucking, and the Turkmen tradition also sounds it by striking the strings quickly with the hand. Its name comes from the Persian for “two strings”, yet the Herat version in Afghanistan can have fourteen strings. It was associated with shepherds in its early period, and in modern use it accompanies singers and is also used in ensembles and instrumental performance, played by the Bauls of Khorasan in Iran and of Bangladesh and West Bengal.
演奏多塔爾琴以右手發聲為主：中國西部維吾爾族多採撥弦，塔吉克、土庫曼、烏茲別克則: The dotar is mostly sounded with the right hand: Uyghurs in western China mainly pluck, while Tajiks, Turkmens and Uzbeks often combine strumming and plucking. The Turkmen tradition neither plucks with the fingers as on a guitar nor with a pick as on a mandolin, but strikes the strings quickly with the palm; because the timbre is soft, the sound has to be kept going by a dense, repeated right-hand motion. A beginner can first tune the two strings a fourth apart in the Turkmen manner, hold the narrow round neck with the fingers, then practise taking a fourth with thumb and middle finger, a fifth with thumb and little finger and a major or minor third with thumb and index finger; the ring finger is mostly used for ornaments.
